status_reason: Full text incl. appendices read; instance optimisation excluded from retained evidence.

paper.title: TextGrad: Automatic "Differentiation" via Text
paper.central_claim: TextGrad performs automatic "differentiation" via text: LLM feedback is backpropagated through computation graphs of text variables to optimise components of compound AI systems (prompts, solutions, code, molecules, treatment plans) with a single general framework.

provenance.notes: actual_model/session_id/receipt_ref not exposed to the worker; null by design (no probing).

rationale: Textual-gradient framework; in-scope prompt optimisation has clean splits and a validation gate but single runs, no ablations, gpt-4o-vs-DSPy mismatch; instance results are non-retained, compute-unmatched, with headline inconsistencies. Retained level; scoped.

missing_sections: figure-embedded numerical content (Figs.1-3, supplementary figures); numeric values in Tables 1-3 are present but duplicated by LaTeX extraction

evidence.quote: TextGrad backpropagates textual feedback provided by LLMs to improve individual components of a compound AI system.
evidence.support_explanation: Central operation.

evidence.quote: developing principled and automated optimization methods for compound AI systems is one of the most important new challenges
evidence.support_explanation: Author gap.

evidence.quote: many of these breakthroughs came from systems that are hand-crafted by experts in the domain of application and are tweaked through heuristics
evidence.support_explanation: Gap: compound systems are hand-tuned.

evidence.quote: Our framework is built on the assumption that the current state-of-the-art LLMs are able to reason about individual components and subtasks of the system that it tries to optimize.
evidence.support_explanation: Explicit assumption.

evidence.quote: Here we use differentiation and gradients as a metaphor for textual feedback from LLMs.
evidence.support_explanation: Gradients are LLM critiques, not mathematical derivatives; no guarantee attached.

evidence.quote: additional language model calls to compute gradients (1 call using the gradient operator for each edge in the computation graph)
evidence.support_explanation: Optimiser cost grows with graph edges; stated as call counts.

evidence.quote: We implement stochastic minibatch gradient descent
evidence.support_explanation: Batch concatenation of per-example critiques.

evidence.quote: we treat not only instructions or demonstrations as variables to optimize, but also the instances we care about themselves
evidence.support_explanation: Instance optimization = per-input test-time refinement (no retained change), outside the retained-component scope.

evidence.quote: while the forward model that performs the reasoning is gpt-3.5-turbo-0125, we use gpt-4o to provide the feedback and improve the prompt
evidence.support_explanation: Prompt optimisation uses a stronger feedback model than the executor.

evidence.quote: After each iteration, we run a validation loop with the validation set of the datasets, and if the performance is better than the previous iteration we update the Prompt.
evidence.support_explanation: Retention gate: prompt updated only if validation score improves.

evidence.quote: We instantiate DSPy’s BootstrappedFewShotRandomSearch (BFSR) optimizer with 10 candidate programs and 8 few-shot examples.
evidence.support_explanation: Alternative optimiser baseline; the teacher/feedback model for BFSR is not stated to be gpt-4o.

evidence.quote: randomly split examples into 50 (training)/100 (validation)/100 (test) samples
evidence.support_explanation: BBH tasks: 100-example test sets.

evidence.quote: which has 200 (training)/300 (validation)/1319 (test) samples
evidence.support_explanation: GSM8K DSPy splits.

evidence.quote: It performs similarly to DSPy [10] for Word Sorting and GSM8k, and improves over DSPy by 7% for Object Counting.
evidence.support_explanation: Honest summary: tie on two of three tasks; difference on one task at n=100 test.

evidence.quote: directly combining the demonstrations from DSPy with the instruction from TextGrad increases the accuracy to 82.1%
evidence.support_explanation: Complementary adjustments; 1 pp on a single run.

evidence.quote: For Word Sorting, we use an LLM to compare the response and the ground truth answer.
evidence.support_explanation: LLM judge (gpt-4o) is the same model family as the gradient engine; judge reliability not validated.

evidence.quote: Table 1: Code optimization for LeetCode Hard using gpt-4o. Results are averaged over 5 seeds.
evidence.support_explanation: Only repeated-run result in the paper (instance optimization).

evidence.quote: We show that these results have now been boosted to 23% for gpt-4o zero-shot and 31% when Reflexion is used.
evidence.support_explanation: Text reports 23% zero-shot while Table 1 lists a zero-shot of 0.26; headline 20% relative gain is not reproduced by 0.36 vs 0.31 (about 16%) (our arithmetic).

evidence.quote: The number of coding problems in LeetCodeHard is 39.
evidence.support_explanation: LeetCode evaluation set of 39 problems.

evidence.quote: it is likely that the dataset we are using in this manuscript is not the same dataset that was used in the Reflexion paper
evidence.support_explanation: Baseline numbers from the cited paper are not on the same data.

evidence.quote: These results show that by spending more computation at test-time through TextGrad self-refinement, we can improve the question answering performance
evidence.support_explanation: Authors acknowledge extra test-time compute; baselines are not compute-matched.

evidence.quote: perform majority voting across all solutions to get the final answer
evidence.support_explanation: TextGrad GPQA answer uses voting over iterations; CoT baseline is a single sample.

evidence.quote: compared to clinical molecules evaluated using the same loss function
evidence.support_explanation: Molecules are optimised directly on the metric on which they are compared; in silico only.

evidence.quote: We compared TextGrad optimized plans with the clinical plans used to treat five prostate cancer patients.
evidence.support_explanation: Five patients; mean and SD of five plans.

evidence.quote: three prostate cancer treatment plans optimized by clinicians, along with their corresponding hyperparameters, are provided
evidence.support_explanation: In-context clinical examples; relation to the evaluation patients is not stated.

evidence.quote: the ultimate test requires experimental and clinical assessments, which are outside of the scope of this paper
evidence.support_explanation: Authors bound the scientific applications.

evidence.quote: Second, greatly inspiring to us, Prompt Optimization with Textual Gradients (ProTeGi) [25] defines the Textual Gradients in the context of prompt optimization
evidence.support_explanation: Closest neighbour for prompt optimisation; no head-to-head comparison.

evidence.quote: both DSPy and ProTeGi focused on prompt optimization, while a significant advance of TextGrad, as demonstrated through our diverse applications, is in instance optimization
evidence.support_explanation: Claimed advance is instance optimisation, not retained-component optimisation.

evidence.quote: The feedback may be noisy, identify what is important and what is correct.
evidence.support_explanation: Optimiser prompt acknowledges noisy critiques; no noise analysis in experiments.

evidence.quote: Meta learning approaches [97, 98, 99] to optimize the TextGrad framework using methods such as TextGrad itself is also an intriguing direction of future work.
evidence.support_explanation: No improver claim is made.

evidence.quote: Across all three tasks, TextGrad improves the performance of the 0-shot prompt significantly.
evidence.support_explanation: Author claim for prompt optimisation without uncertainty.

signatures.object: System prompt of a weaker executor LLM (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125); baseline: zero-shot CoT prompt and DSPy BFSR demonstrations
signatures.information: Per-example conversation (system prompt, input, output) and an evaluation signal against ground truth; gpt-4o as backward engine; 36 sampled training examples
signatures.operation: Forward minibatch (3 examples) -> loss per example -> backward: LLM critique of the prompt in context -> TGD step rewrites the prompt; accept only if validation improves
signatures.conditions: Labels available at train time; stronger feedback model
signatures.feedback: Ground-truth correctness (string match or gpt-4o judge)
signatures.selection_rule/data: Validation improvement gate per iteration; 50/100/100 BBH and 200/300/1319 GSM8K splits
signatures.claimed_effect: Prompt optimisation matches DSPy on 2 of 3 tasks and exceeds it on Object Counting; all exceed zero-shot CoT
signatures.failure_boundary: No component ablation; noisy critiques; no rollback beyond the validation gate

signatures.object: Single-instance variables (code, solutions, SMILES, radiotherapy hyperparameters) - test-time refinement per input
signatures.information: Evaluator output, unit tests, docking simulator, matRad plans
signatures.operation: Iterate critique-and-rewrite on the instance for a few steps; majority vote for QA
signatures.claimed_effect: LeetCode-Hard 0.36 vs Reflexion 0.31; GPQA 55%; molecules; treatment plans

gap.author_gap: Compound AI systems are hand-crafted and heuristically tuned; there is no principled, turn-key automatic optimisation analogous to backpropagation for neural networks.
gap.checked_gap: Real. Closest neighbours (DSPy, ProTeGi textual gradients, OPRO-type LLM optimisers, Reflexion/Self-Refine) are named and distinguished by generality, but TextGrad is not compared with ProTeGi or OPRO in the prompt-optimisation experiments, and multi-component credit assignment through a graph is not demonstrated.
gap.lineage/closest_adjacent: ProTeGi (textual gradients for prompts), DSPy (programs, demonstrations), LLM-as-optimizer prompt tuners, Reflexion/Self-Refine (per-instance self-improvement).
gap.residue: No unified framework to backpropagate feedback across variables of a compound system.
gap.method_response: Computation graph of text variables, backward LLM critique along edges, TGD step with batching, constraints and momentum.
gap.remaining_gap: No evidence the graph propagation (vs a single critique) is the active ingredient; no ablations; no compute-matched baselines.
gap.unresolved: ProTeGi, OPRO and Self-Refine were not read here; novelty relative to them is author-asserted.

matches.tactic_steps_checked: Identify an unsolved problem (non-differentiable compound-system optimisation), recast it as a computation graph with a backward pass and an optimiser step, and apply the autodiff toolbox (batching, momentum, constraints): executed as an analogy. No reduction or guarantee is proved; the solver is an LLM heuristic.
matches.success_failure_checks: RE-1 (prove the reduction) unmet; RE-2 (formally define the object) met for the graph/variable abstractions; RE-3 (new identifying structure) partial; RE-4 (faithfulness validation) unmet; RE-6 (actionable principle) met.
matches.reason: Sub null: C00/C21/C27 reformulate transparency questions, RL as supervised learning and games; none matches.

matches.tactic_steps_checked: Textual gradients are model-generated feedback used as the adaptation signal; for instance optimisation the loss is self-supervised, for prompts it uses labels.
matches.success_failure_checks: RE-2 (ablate to attribute gain to the manufactured signal) unmet.
matches.reason: Different operation: model-generated critique as signal.

rs_pattern.resolves_problem_reason: Prompt-level gains over zero-shot CoT are shown on three tasks; general optimisation of compound systems via graph propagation is not demonstrated (no multi-node results, no ablation).

matches.condition_checks: The prompt-optimisation experiments hold a single system prompt as the incumbent and rewrite it from per-example critiques (H10). Step 1 successes+failures: critiques come from all batch items; step 3 localised edit: whole prompt rewrite (partial); retention gate: validation improvement (met); held-out split: met. Taxonomy note moves single-prompt TG work to H10.

The framework defines propagation through a graph (equation 11, Algorithm 1), but no experiment optimises more than one interacting variable through graph propagation with attribution scope choice; S1 (scope) untested, H09 step 5 certification partial.

unassigned: Per-instance refinement (code, solutions, molecules, plans) is test-time self-refinement without a retained component and falls outside the harness scope.

pattern_mapping.operation_correspondence: RS: recast optimisation of a compound system as a graph with backward pass and optimiser; RSI H09: model system as an executed graph and route component-specific critique to upstream nodes, update jointly, gate updates.
pattern_mapping.necessary_conditions_differences: H09 requires scope-bounded propagation and gating of structural proposals; the paper implements the abstraction but evaluates it with single-variable graphs.

pattern_mapping.operation_correspondence: RS: model-generated feedback as signal; RSI H10: textual-gradient critique rewrites the incumbent prompt.
pattern_mapping.necessary_conditions_differences: H10 expects gating on previously correct examples and cluster-level aggregation; only a validation-improvement gate and batch concatenation exist.

expectations.reason: Analogy to backpropagation is explicit as a metaphor; no equivalence or guarantee.
Graph/variable/optimizer abstractions are new packaging of critique-and-rewrite; gains over ProTeGi-style single critique are untested.
No test that propagated critiques localise to the responsible variable.

expectations.applies_when: attribute gains to the manufactured signal
expectations.reason: No ablation of backward feedback vs random edits, nor of momentum/batching/constraints.
Calls per iteration are stated; no totals or comparison with baselines.
No experiment varies attribution scope in a multi-variable graph.
Validation-improvement gate prevents regressions on validation; no per-example regression check.
Full conversation (system prompt, input, output) and objective are provided to the backward engine.
Prompt optimisation uses labels; instance optimisation for QA uses self-evaluation only and Word Sorting accuracy uses an LLM judge from the feedback model family.

expectations.applies_when: feedback assumed to isolate the edited artifact
expectations.reason: Critiques on the prompt are not checked for whether the failure was caused by the prompt.

expectations.applies_when: critique-rewrite loops report held-out score and baselines
expectations.reason: Held-out test and alternative optimiser (DSPy) reported; teacher models differ and no same-budget comparison.

expectations.applies_when: comparing prompt optimisers with different feedback models
expectations.reason: TextGrad uses gpt-4o as backward/update engine while the DSPy baseline is not stated to use a gpt-4o teacher; number of LM calls differs.
Prompt optimisation has no seeds or intervals; only LeetCode reports five seeds.

expectations.applies_when: abstract and tables report the same quantities
expectations.reason: LeetCode zero-shot differs between text (23%) and table (0.26); 20% relative gain not reproduced by 0.36 vs 0.31.
SOTA-type claims rest on voting-based test-time compute (GPQA), a re-extracted 39-problem dataset and in silico metrics optimised directly.

claims.text: Prompt optimisation with TextGrad improves gpt-3.5-turbo reasoning over zero-shot CoT and matches or beats DSPy.
claims.setting: Object Counting, Word Sorting (BBH 50/100/100), GSM8K (200/300/1319); gpt-3.5 executor, gpt-4o feedback
claims.baseline/control: zero-shot CoT; DSPy BFSR (10 candidates, 8 demos)
claims.selection_vs_test: validation gate per iteration; test reported
claims.result/denominator: tie on Word Sorting and GSM8K, +7 pp on Object Counting (n=100)
claims.allowed_conclusion: A gpt-4o-guided prompt rewrite loop raised held-out accuracy over zero-shot on three tasks; superiority over DSPy is not established.

claims.text: TextGrad is a general framework for optimising compound AI systems by backpropagating text through graphs.
claims.result/denominator: no multi-variable graph optimisation result; results are single-variable
claims.allowed_conclusion: Demonstrated as a library of single-variable critique-rewrite loops; graph propagation benefit untested.

claims.text: Instance optimisation improves coding (LeetCode-Hard 0.36), QA (GPQA 55%), molecules and treatment plans.
claims.baseline/control: Reflexion, CoT, best reported, clinical plans
claims.result/denominator: 39 problems x 5 seeds; GPQA 198; MMLU subsets 112/92; 5 patients
claims.allowed_conclusion: Task-level test-time gains with extra compute; outside the retained-component scope.

assessment.evidence_level_reason: For the prompt-optimisation experiments, a retained prompt (selected with validation) improves held-out test accuracy; instance-optimisation results are task-level only.
assessment.strongest_supported_claim: On BBH Object Counting, Word Sorting and GSM8K, a gpt-4o-driven textual-gradient rewrite of the system prompt of gpt-3.5-turbo (accepted only if validation improved) beat zero-shot CoT on held-out tests and tied or exceeded DSPy BFSR (author-reported, single runs).
assessment.unresolved: Graph-propagation benefit, ablations, compute-matched baselines, comparison with ProTeGi/OPRO, uncertainty.

retention_trace.proposed_change: gpt-4o textual-gradient rewrite of the system prompt from batches of 3 examples
retention_trace.selection: accept if validation score improves; 12 iterations
retention_trace.measured_gain: GSM8K 72.9 -> 81.1 and Object Counting 77.8 -> 91.9 (author-reported); instance tasks have no retention
retention_trace.gaps: no ablation, no variance, no compute-matched baselines

scope_note: Instance-optimisation experiments (coding, QA, molecules, treatment plans) are per-input refinement without a retained component; scored only as supplementary task-level evidence.

G.reason: Concrete, important gap (turn-key optimisation of hand-tuned compound systems) with the closest prompt-optimisation neighbours (DSPy, ProTeGi) named and distinguished; neither ProTeGi nor OPRO is compared, and the claimed advance is largely instance optimisation, which is outside retained harness scope.

M.reason: Operations, information flow and assumptions (LLMs can critique components, noisy feedback) are specified and reconstructable; the backprop analogy is metaphorical, graph propagation is not shown to differ from a single critique, and no distinguishable prediction against ProTeGi-style rewriting is offered.

X.reason: Algorithm 1, backward and optimizer prompts, batching, momentum, constraints and the validation gate are given with hyper-parameters (batch 3, 12 iterations); failure and noise boundaries, regression handling beyond the validation gate and which iterate is reported for instance tasks are not stated.

E.measurement.reason: Exact-match and platform-test metrics are objective, but Word Sorting is judged by gpt-4o (same family as the feedback engine), headline LeetCode numbers disagree between abstract, text and table, and the baseline dataset differs from the cited paper.

E.causality.reason: Zero-shot CoT starting prompt is a clean control for prompt optimisation and DSPy is an alternative optimiser, but no component ablation exists, the gpt-4o feedback engine differs from the DSPy setup, budgets are not matched and graph propagation is never isolated.

E.holdout.reason: Prompt optimisation has train/validation/test separation, but claims of generality and state-of-the-art rest on per-input refinement with extra compute, a re-extracted 39-problem set, in silico metrics optimised directly, and five patients with in-context clinical examples of unclear relation to the evaluation plans.

E.statistics.reason: Test sizes are stated (100, 1319, 39, 5) and LeetCode alone is averaged over five seeds, but the in-scope prompt-optimisation results are single numbers on 100-example tests with no seeds or intervals while a 7 pp gap and ties are interpreted.

E.cost.reason: Calls per iteration are described (one per edge, three per iteration for coding/QA) and extra test-time compute is acknowledged, but no totals in tokens or dollars are given and the baselines are neither compute- nor feedback-model-matched.
